newsitem.title: UK: Most bets off as funds seek U.S. rate clarity - poll.
newsitem.headline: Most bets off as funds seek U.S. rate clarity - poll.

text.p: Global fund managers remain underweight in U.S. equities amid interest rate concerns, but many are stumped for clear alternatives due to liquidity fears and global market uncertainty.
A Reuters monthly global asset allocation survey of mostly UK-based fund managers showed a continued underweight U.S. equity position, with Europe benefiting most from the strategy.
"It is difficult to take big bets at the moment," said Michael Hughes, global market strategist at BZW. "Until the clarity with U.S. interest rate policy improves we are just hanging back a bit."
Managers said that U.S. long bond yields above seven percent remained tempting, but were insufficient to spark a major shift in allocation away from equity markets.
"Equities will not get the bond rug pulled from under them," said Shaun Roache, investment strategist at ING Barings.
He said they would retain a degree of support through the year, although with near term volatility, while U.S. bond yields should stabilise and begin to drift down through the next 12 months.
"Although equities will suffer from relatively poor earnings growth compared to the past two years, they won't be undermined from a relative valuation standpoint," he said.
Hughes said he was positive about UK gilts versus continental Europe, and similarly U.S. yields above seven percent made them more attractive relative to Europe.
But he said general uncertainty about U.S. interest rates was unlikely to recede in the near term.

"We are looking for signs that nominal income growth in the U.S. is moving into a four to five percent range which we think the Fed will be more comfortable with, and we are looking for signs that the interest rate risks further down the road are no higher than are contained in the forward yield curve.
"Clearly if the interest rate risks in the U.S. are greater than we are assuming then I am going to rein in my emerging market bets and I have got to have more of a cash and equity bias."

Roache said long bonds above seven percent were a buying opportunity, especially as that market had been factoring in a lot of bad news in the past few weeks. The likelihood of a protracted U.S. rate rise was limited.
He said the U.S. equity market was likely to underperform relatively over the year.
He was positive on Europe, moving towards the core from the periphery as a lot of the EMU convergence has already been achieved.

"On a medium term view the core is positioned to perform well because of the degree of corporate restructuring in Germany, France and the Netherlands. There is going to be a bit of earnings momentum there throughout the next few years, certainly the next 12 months."
Goldman Sachs' portfolio strategy team said the lack of synchronisation in the economic cycles of the major economies pointed to a decoupling of market performances in the coming months.

"While the U.S. is clearly running into capacity constraints which could require higher interest rates, continental Europe and Japan still have spare capacity and probably do not need to raise interest rates for some time."
With Japan and Europe forecast to remain below potential output into 1998 and the U.S. facing capacity constraints, it said Japan and Europe were probably better bets than the U.S.

"Our view of the economic and interest rate cycles points to an underweight position in the economy most advanced in the cycle, the U.S., favouring markets less advanced in the cycle, continental Europe and Japan," Goldman Sachs said.

Roache said U.S. mutual fund flows would be closely watched after U.S. domestic market inflows of about $20 billion in December and January slowed in February, resulting in the biggest drop in monthly net inflows in history.
He said mutual funds' high sensitivity to long term interest rates has caused volatility in the near term.
"Given that we see long bond yields drifting down over the next 12 months, U.S. liquidity will remain supportive on a 12 month view, although maybe not at the heights we saw at the end of 1996."
